ch01_introduction/fig01_density_vs_press.mechanism: Compression reduces the volume occupied by a fixed gas mass; real-gas interactions make the density change nonlinear.
ch01_introduction/fig01_density_vs_press.implication: A fixed mass flow can impose a much larger actual-volume load on low-pressure piping and compressor suction equipment.
ch01_introduction/fig01_density_vs_press.recommendation: Use actual inlet density at each operating case when converting mass rate to velocity, vessel gas load and compressor inlet volume.

ch01_introduction/fig02_z_factor_vs_pres.mechanism: Attractive interactions initially reduce gas volume below the ideal-gas prediction; repulsive effects become more important as pressure increases.
ch01_introduction/fig02_z_factor_vs_pres.implication: A constant Z can distort standard-to-actual volume conversion and the pressure dependence of available throughput.
ch01_introduction/fig02_z_factor_vs_pres.recommendation: Evaluate Z at the local temperature, pressure and composition along the system rather than applying a single standard-condition value.

ch01_introduction/fig03_phase_envelope.p.mechanism: The saturation boundary identifies states where a second hydrocarbon phase can first appear; it is a thermodynamic boundary, not an operating trajectory.
ch01_introduction/fig03_phase_envelope.p.implication: Expansion and cooling can cross into two-phase flow even when the upstream stream is a single gas phase.
ch01_introduction/fig03_phase_envelope.p.recommendation: Overlay the actual operating path and uncertainty envelope, using only finite traced branches and the contract pressure basis for dew-point limits.

ch01_introduction/fig04_production_sensi.mechanism: Lower wellhead backpressure can increase reservoir drawdown, while tubing and downstream pressure losses oppose the resulting rate increase.
ch01_introduction/fig04_production_sensi.implication: The marginal benefit of pressure reduction depends on the coupled well and facility constraints, not reservoir pressure alone.
ch01_introduction/fig04_production_sensi.recommendation: Reconcile the sensitivity with an IPR–tubing operating-point calculation and check downstream handling capacity before selecting a pressure target.

ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig01_den.mechanism: SRK and Peng–Robinson use different cubic-EOS attraction and covolume expressions, so they predict different real-fluid volumes for the same composition.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig01_den.implication: The difference is a model-form sensitivity; agreement between two models is not independent experimental validation.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig01_den.recommendation: Compare the alternatives against measured PVT density over the intended envelope and carry the validated model into capacity calculations.

ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig02_cp_.mechanism: Heat capacity measures the enthalpy response to temperature at fixed pressure and varies with molecular degrees of freedom and non-ideal interactions.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig02_cp_.implication: A constant heat-capacity estimate may misstate heater duty or the temperature rise associated with compressor work.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig02_cp_.recommendation: Use stream enthalpy differences for equipment energy balances and treat a constant Cp only as a local screening approximation.

ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig03_ent.mechanism: The slope of an isobaric enthalpy curve is heat capacity; changes in phase distribution can add a latent-heat contribution.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig03_ent.implication: Duty is determined by the difference between inlet and outlet enthalpy, not the absolute value of an arbitrarily referenced enthalpy.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig03_ent.recommendation: Keep the same composition, flow basis and reference convention when calculating duty, and examine phase changes before fitting a straight line.

ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig04_vis.mechanism: Increasing gas density changes molecular momentum transport and therefore viscosity; the relationship is not the same as liquid-viscosity behavior.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig04_vis.implication: Viscosity affects Reynolds number, friction factor and ultimately the distribution of pressure losses.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig04_vis.recommendation: Initialize transport properties and recalculate them at local pipeline states when checking hydraulic capacity.

ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig05_jt_.mechanism: The Joule–Thomson coefficient is the local temperature derivative with respect to pressure along a constant-enthalpy path.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig05_jt_.implication: A positive coefficient predicts cooling for a pressure drop, but its changing magnitude prevents applying one inlet value over a large letdown.
ch02_thermodynamic_foundations/fig05_jt_.recommendation: Use a PH flash for a finite valve pressure drop and inspect condensation and hydrate proximity along the resulting path.

ch03_fluid_characterization/fig01_molecu.mechanism: Heavy-end characterization distributes an unresolved fraction into pseudo-components with assigned molecular weights and densities.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig01_molecu.implication: The assumed tail controls liquid density, vapor–liquid equilibrium and predicted condensate recovery even when the total plus fraction is unchanged.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig01_molecu.recommendation: Constrain the distribution with measured plus-fraction molecular weight, density and boiling data; retain the characterization settings with the fluid model.

ch03_fluid_characterization/fig02_phase_.mechanism: Heavy hydrocarbons extend the saturation envelope and make gas-condensate phase behavior sensitive to the uncertain C7+ tail.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig02_phase_.implication: A traced dew branch can be useful even when the solver cannot produce a complete bubble branch; an absent branch must not be replaced by an invented curve.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig02_phase_.recommendation: Validate dew pressure and liquid dropout against laboratory data and distinguish calculated branch coverage from the full physical envelope.

ch03_fluid_characterization/fig03_liquid.mechanism: At fixed composition, successive equilibrium flashes show how the liquid volume changes as pressure traverses the two-phase region.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig03_liquid.implication: A fixed-composition pressure sweep does not reproduce a constant-volume depletion experiment, which removes gas and changes the remaining composition.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig03_liquid.recommendation: Use the curve as a phase-behavior screen; use NeqSim’s actual depletion experiment model when comparing with CVD laboratory data.

ch03_fluid_characterization/fig04_gor_vs.mechanism: Pressure reduction transfers volatile components from the hydrocarbon liquid into the equilibrium gas phase.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig04_gor_vs.implication: An equilibrium phase gas-to-oil ratio is sensitive to the chosen reference volumes and is not automatically the solution GOR reported by a separator or differential-liberation test.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig04_gor_vs.recommendation: State the volume basis and separation procedure, and match those definitions before comparing with laboratory Rs or field GOR.

ch03_fluid_characterization/fig05_bo_vs_.mechanism: Oil formation volume factor compares reservoir oil volume with the stock-tank oil volume obtained from the same material after a specified surface separation.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig05_bo_vs_.implication: Using unrelated fluids or inconsistent flash histories in the numerator and denominator produces an apparent Bo with no material-balance meaning.
ch03_fluid_characterization/fig05_bo_vs_.recommendation: Track the same oil sample through reservoir and stock-tank flashes and report the reference temperature, pressure and separation path.

ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig01_ip.mechanism: An IPR relates liquid or gas deliverability to drawdown; curvature reflects the selected inflow law and reservoir phase behavior.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig01_ip.implication: A high zero-backpressure intercept does not establish a producible operating rate because tubing and facility backpressure still have to be satisfied.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig01_ip.recommendation: Calibrate the appropriate inflow law against well tests and intersect it with a verified tubing relationship on the same rate and pressure basis.

ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig02_go.mechanism: As pressure falls, dissolved light components evolve into a gas phase and change the gas and liquid volumes.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig02_go.implication: Gas-handling demand can increase relative to oil rate during depletion; a static initial GOR can therefore understate future bottlenecks.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig02_go.recommendation: Distinguish fixed-composition flashes from depletion with gas withdrawal, and couple the appropriate PVT path to separator and compression capacity.

ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig03_de.mechanism: Depth changes both hydrostatic pressure and temperature; these effects jointly alter fluid density.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig03_de.implication: A constant-density hydrostatic approximation can bias bottom-hole pressure, particularly for compressible or near-saturation fluids.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig03_de.recommendation: Integrate density over the pressure–temperature path and compare with measured gradients before using the profile for well control or inflow calibration.

ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig04_re.mechanism: The Corey curves allocate effective flow capacity between phases according to saturation, residual saturation and fitted exponents.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig04_re.implication: Their endpoints and curvature can control water breakthrough and mobility predictions; the plotted curves are constitutive assumptions rather than EOS results.
ch04_reservoir_engineering/ch04_fig04_re.recommendation: Replace the illustrative parameters with rock-type-specific core data and examine hysteresis and endpoint uncertainty in reservoir forecasts.

ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig01_vlp_cur.mechanism: Tubing pressure loss combines hydrostatic head, wall friction and acceleration; changing diameter alters friction and liquid transport.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig01_vlp_cur.implication: A diameter that reduces friction at high rate may increase liquid loading or change the low-rate operating branch.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig01_vlp_cur.recommendation: Compare feasible IPR intersections for each diameter and reject trials with nonpositive outlet pressure or inconsistent upward elevation sign.

ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig02_operati.mechanism: The operating point is the rate at which reservoir deliverability and the tubing pressure requirement satisfy the same bottom-hole boundary.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig02_operati.implication: The root residual quantifies whether the selected rate actually delivers the required wellhead pressure; visual proximity alone is insufficient.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig02_operati.recommendation: Check the pressure residual, BHP greater than WHP for upward production, and sensitivity to IPR and hydraulic-correlation uncertainty.

ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig03_gas_lif.mechanism: Injected gas reduces the hydrostatic density of the wellbore mixture while increasing friction and surface gas handling.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig03_gas_lif.implication: Improved lift pressure does not by itself establish incremental oil production; a rate gain requires a coupled inflow solution and sufficient gas capacity.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig03_gas_lif.recommendation: Optimize gas allocation using incremental oil or value per unit injection gas, including compression demand and total gas availability.

ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig04_watercu.mechanism: Increasing water fraction changes mixture density, liquid holdup and friction while reducing the oil fraction of the produced stream.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig04_watercu.implication: At a fixed total mass rate, oil production and available lifting margin can both deteriorate as water cut rises.
ch05_well_performance/ch05_fig04_watercu.recommendation: Track oil, gas and water rates separately and recompute the coupled well operating point at each water-cut case.

ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_choke_s.mechanism: At imposed upstream flow, closing a fixed-Cv choke requires more pressure drop; sufficiently restricted openings may have no feasible positive outlet pressure.
ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_choke_s.implication: This pressure-mode experiment is not a prediction that the same well rate remains deliverable at every opening.
ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_choke_s.recommendation: Reject infeasible pressure solutions and use the coupled reservoir–tubing–network model when translating a choke opening into a production rate.

ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_well_ne.mechanism: Each well’s pressure budget depends on its inlet condition and the resistance of its branch to the common manifold.
ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_well_ne.implication: The well with the highest wellhead pressure is not necessarily the largest contributor once branch losses and common backpressure are included.
ch06_wells_artificial_lift/ch15w_well_ne.recommendation: Compare branch residuals and rates on one basis before adjusting chokes or assigning a debottlenecking priority.

ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.mechanism: Friction and elevation redistribute pressure along the subsea route; changing density and phase holdup alters the local gradient.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.implication: The arrival pressure determines how much pressure is available for the riser and receiving plant, rather than constituting a free design input.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.recommendation: Use the surveyed elevation profile, verify the pressure budget and refine segmentation until the arrival pressure is stable.

ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.mechanism: Heat exchange drives the flowing fluid toward seabed temperature while pressure change and phase behavior modify the thermal response.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.implication: A calculated arrival temperature is conditional on heat-transfer assumptions and flow rate; it cannot establish shutdown cooldown time.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.recommendation: Calibrate the overall heat-transfer coefficient and evaluate low-flow and shutdown cases separately from the steady-state profile.

ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.mechanism: Hydrate equilibrium depends on local pressure, gas composition and water activity; the operating path adds the route’s heat and pressure losses.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.implication: Crossing the equilibrium boundary indicates thermodynamic hydrate stability when free water is available, not an instantaneous plugging prediction.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.recommendation: Apply a stated operating margin and evaluate water availability, inhibitor concentration, cooldown and restart conditions before selecting protection measures.

ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.mechanism: Superficial gas and liquid velocities characterize the competing inertia, buoyancy and phase-continuity mechanisms that form flow regimes.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.implication: A horizontal regime map is a screening tool and may not describe inclined sections, risers or transient severe slugging.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.recommendation: Use regime labels within the correlation’s domain and assess liquid accumulation and transient slugging for the actual route.

ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.mechanism: The total well-to-platform pressure difference is consumed by tubing lift, choke loss, flowline friction and riser elevation.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.implication: A negative passive choke loss or a booster with negative power exposes an inconsistent model boundary rather than a production benefit.
ch07_subsea_production_systems/ch06_fig0.recommendation: Check each pressure contribution and the sign of equipment work before allocating additional backpressure or evaluating subsea boosting.

ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig01_pressure.mechanism: A larger bore reduces velocity and frictional pressure loss at fixed rate; density, holdup and friction-factor changes modify the simple diameter scaling.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig01_pressure.implication: A small increase in bore can recover pressure margin, but excessive size may affect low-rate liquid transport and project cost.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig01_pressure.recommendation: Select a diameter from the feasible arrival-pressure envelope and check turndown, holdup, erosion and installation constraints.

ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig02_pressure.mechanism: Raising mass flow increases velocity, friction and possibly acceleration losses as the gas expands along the line.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig02_pressure.implication: The pressure-drop trend can steepen near the hydraulic limit; a failed forward solve is not a valid high-flow data point.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig02_pressure.recommendation: Bracket the feasible flow interval, retain failure diagnostics and solve the arrival-pressure boundary directly when determining capacity.

ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig03_liquid_h.mechanism: Gas shear and liquid slip compete with gravity to determine the amount of liquid retained in the pipe.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig03_liquid_h.implication: Holdup is a local flow-correlation result and differs from the inlet liquid fraction; it affects both hydrostatic loss and liquid inventory.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig03_liquid_h.recommendation: Compare the selected correlation with representative operating data and examine the low-gas-rate regime for liquid accumulation.

ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig04_pipeline.mechanism: The hydraulic capacity is a boundary solution: the maximum feasible rate satisfying the available pressure-drop or arrival-pressure constraint.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig04_pipeline.implication: If the numerical search stops at its rate bound, the resulting point is a bound-limited result rather than a demonstrated pipeline limit.
ch08_flowlines_and_risers/fig04_pipeline.recommendation: Expand the bracket where needed and report active pressure limits, residuals and the feasibility of the final trial.

ch09_flow_assurance/fig01_hydrate_equili.mechanism: Higher pressure stabilizes gas hydrates at higher temperature for the specified gas and aqueous phase.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig01_hydrate_equili.implication: The equilibrium curve defines thermodynamic susceptibility; it does not predict formation time, deposition rate or plug location.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig01_hydrate_equili.recommendation: Use a validated fluid and water model, enable hydrate checking, and combine the boundary with route temperatures and an explicit operating margin.

ch09_flow_assurance/fig02_meg_inhibition.mechanism: MEG lowers water activity and depresses hydrate equilibrium temperature; the relevant concentration is in the aqueous phase.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig02_meg_inhibition.implication: An injection percentage on total wellstream flow is not interchangeable with the required aqueous MEG concentration.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig02_meg_inhibition.recommendation: Close the water–MEG mass balance through condensation, produced-water influx and regeneration before setting an inhibitor rate.

ch09_flow_assurance/fig03_water_dewpoint.mechanism: The water dew point is the saturation temperature corresponding to the specified gas water content at each pressure.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig03_water_dewpoint.implication: A fixed ppmv water content has a pressure-dependent dew point, so dehydration compliance must use the contractual pressure basis.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig03_water_dewpoint.recommendation: Reject solver sentinel temperatures and verify the ppmv, mg/Sm3 and standard-volume reference conversions when comparing with measurements.

ch09_flow_assurance/fig04_hydrate_operat.mechanism: The distance between the operating path and hydrate boundary reflects the combined effects of cooling, pressure loss and inhibition.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig04_hydrate_operat.implication: A nominal warm steady-state case can conceal vulnerability during turndown, shutdown or restart.
ch09_flow_assurance/fig04_hydrate_operat.recommendation: Evaluate the full operating envelope, including uncertainty and transient cooldown, and document the minimum temperature margin along the route.

ch10_separation_technology/fig01_phase_s.mechanism: Separator pressure and temperature determine the equilibrium distribution of feed components among gas, oil and water.
ch10_separation_technology/fig01_phase_s.implication: An equilibrium phase split gives available phase quantities; it does not determine droplet carry-over, emulsion breakage or solids removal.
ch10_separation_technology/fig01_phase_s.recommendation: Combine the flash result with residence time, internals performance and a mass-balance check when assessing separator operation.

ch10_separation_technology/fig02_souders.mechanism: The density difference between the dispersed liquid and gas sets the gravitational separation tendency represented by the Souders–Brown relation.
ch10_separation_technology/fig02_souders.implication: The same gas mass rate produces different gas velocity and required area as pressure changes; a fixed K-factor alone does not define complete capacity.
ch10_separation_technology/fig02_souders.recommendation: Evaluate K-factor applicability, gas area and demister limitations at each operating pressure using a fixed physical vessel geometry.

ch10_separation_technology/fig03_separat.mechanism: Changing intermediate pressure redistributes light components between vented gas and the liquid passed to later separation stages.
ch10_separation_technology/fig03_separat.implication: The best pressure for liquid recovery may differ from the best pressure for export quality, recompression duty or total value.
ch10_separation_technology/fig03_separat.recommendation: Optimize against the complete separation train and a consistent stock-tank reference, with vapor-pressure and compression constraints included.

ch10_separation_technology/fig04_separat.mechanism: Successive pressure reductions liberate additional gas and change the composition and volume of the residual liquid.
ch10_separation_technology/fig04_separat.implication: Later-stage gas and liquid handling can become limiting even when the first separator has spare capacity.
ch10_separation_technology/fig04_separat.recommendation: Close phase mass balances across every stage and distinguish the final separator liquid rate from a properly flashed stock-tank oil rate.

ch11_oil_processing/fig10_1_rvp_vs_tempe.mechanism: Stabilization heating removes volatile components, changing the equilibrium vapor pressure of the remaining oil at the reporting temperature.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_1_rvp_vs_tempe.implication: This bubble-point-based quantity is TVP; it must not be presented as an ASTM RVP result merely because the calculation uses 37.8°C.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_1_rvp_vs_tempe.recommendation: Specify the product sampling and vapor-pressure method, then choose duty with a quality margin and a corresponding liquid-recovery calculation.

ch11_oil_processing/fig10_2_api_vs_press.mechanism: Separator pressure changes which light components remain in the oil; its reference-temperature density changes accordingly.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_2_api_vs_press.implication: API gravity is meaningful only at its defined density reference basis, and changes in API alone do not quantify saleable oil recovery.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_2_api_vs_press.recommendation: Calculate the oil sample density at 60°F and compare gravity together with stabilized oil volume and vapor pressure.

ch11_oil_processing/fig10_3_multistage_o.mechanism: Additional equilibrium separation stages alter the release of light components and the final liquid composition.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_3_multistage_o.implication: Stage count alone does not determine oil quality or optimal recovery; stage pressures and heat input remain part of the specification.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_3_multistage_o.recommendation: Compare alternatives at the same final oil-quality target and include the recompression and heating duties of the added stages.

ch11_oil_processing/fig10_4_gas_shrinkag.mechanism: Gas liberation at successive pressure reductions changes the amount and composition of material retained as liquid.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_4_gas_shrinkag.implication: A pressure-sweep phase split is not the same experiment as differential liberation unless evolved gas is explicitly withdrawn at every step.
ch11_oil_processing/fig10_4_gas_shrinkag.recommendation: State whether the material is recombined or depleted between points, and reconcile liberated gas and remaining oil with the overall material balance.

ch12_gas_processing/fig11_1_water_conten.mechanism: Warmer gas in equilibrium with liquid water can carry more water vapor, with pressure and gas composition affecting saturation.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_1_water_conten.implication: Cooling upstream of a dehydration unit may remove bulk water but does not establish the low water content required for export.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_1_water_conten.recommendation: Specify both saturation state and water-content units, and use a separate dehydration calculation and dew-point check for the treated gas.

ch12_gas_processing/fig11_2_jt_cooling.p.mechanism: Adiabatic throttling conserves enthalpy while pressure reduction changes temperature and potentially condenses liquids.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_2_jt_cooling.p.implication: Cooling duty and liquid recovery vary with the full inlet state, so a single constant Joule–Thomson coefficient cannot represent every pressure ratio.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_2_jt_cooling.p.recommendation: Run a PH flash for each letdown case and verify cold-separator load, hydrate margin and the need for gas recompression.

ch12_gas_processing/fig11_3_turbo_expand.mechanism: The expander removes shaft work from the gas, lowering its enthalpy; subsequent separation redistributes the condensed liquids.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_3_turbo_expand.implication: The temperature profile depends on expansion efficiency and stage boundary conditions, not only on the overall pressure drop.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_3_turbo_expand.recommendation: Close the process energy balance and check expander liquid tolerance, minimum temperature and recovered-power use.

ch12_gas_processing/fig11_4_dewpoint_con.mechanism: Lower cold-separator temperature transfers heavier hydrocarbons preferentially to liquid and changes the residual C2+ and C3+ gas fractions.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_4_dewpoint_con.implication: Composition reduction is an indicator of treatment severity, but the actual hydrocarbon dew point must still be calculated at the contract pressure.
ch12_gas_processing/fig11_4_dewpoint_con.recommendation: Choose the least-cost feasible cooling level using both gas quality and recovered-liquid value, including pressure loss and recompression demand.

ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_water.mechanism: Rising water cut redirects produced-fluid handling capacity from hydrocarbon liquid toward water, with phase densities affecting mass-to-volume conversions.
ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_water.implication: Total liquid throughput can remain large while oil production falls, making water treatment and disposal the active constraints.
ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_water.recommendation: Report oil and water rates separately and evaluate treatment residence time, injection capacity and oil-in-water performance at late-life water cuts.

ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_press.mechanism: Changing separator pressure alters gas liberation from the hydrocarbon phase and the equilibrium phase split of the mixed feed.
ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_press.implication: The flash alone does not predict dispersed oil removal efficiency, emulsion behavior or the discharge water’s measured oil concentration.
ch13_produced_water_treatment/ch16_press.recommendation: Use the calculated phase rates as loads for a treatment train, then apply validated separation-efficiency and water-quality models.

ch14_gas_compression/fig12_1_power_vs_ra.mechanism: Increasing pressure ratio raises required specific compression work; lower polytropic efficiency increases both shaft demand and heating.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_1_power_vs_ra.implication: A driver power limit and a discharge-temperature limit may constrain different parts of the same operating envelope.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_1_power_vs_ra.recommendation: Activate polytropic calculation explicitly, check both limits at the actual gas composition and retain an ambient-dependent driver margin.

ch14_gas_compression/fig12_2_compressor_.mechanism: A compressor map relates head and efficiency to inlet volume and rotational speed; the plotted map is an illustrative performance model.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_2_compressor_.implication: Synthetic curve shape cannot establish a real machine’s surge line, choke limit or guaranteed efficiency.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_2_compressor_.recommendation: Replace the teaching map with a vendor or validated test map, including its flow, head, efficiency and correction-condition definitions.

ch14_gas_compression/fig12_3_multistage_.mechanism: Each compressor raises gas temperature, while intercooling lowers the inlet temperature and specific work of the following stage.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_3_multistage_.implication: The highest stage discharge temperature, rather than the final cooled outlet, must meet the thermal limit; the updated three-stage example slightly exceeds the illustrative 150°C limit.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_3_multistage_.recommendation: Adjust stage count, intermediate pressures or cooling conditions and recheck every stage before accepting the train configuration.

ch14_gas_compression/fig12_4_power_compa.mechanism: Intercooling reduces the average specific volume during compression and therefore lowers total work relative to one hot compression step.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_4_power_compa.implication: The power benefit has diminishing returns and must be weighed against additional equipment, pressure losses and maintenance.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_4_power_compa.recommendation: Compare stage alternatives with consistent efficiency and cooling assumptions, then include total driver power, temperature limits and lifecycle cost.

ch14_gas_compression/fig12_5_discharge_t.mechanism: Compression converts shaft work into fluid enthalpy; a lower efficiency produces a larger temperature rise for the same pressure ratio.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_5_discharge_t.implication: A feasible pressure target may still require another stage or more effective intercooling because of material, lubricant or process-temperature limits.
ch14_gas_compression/fig12_5_discharge_t.recommendation: Apply the project-specific temperature limit to every operating and degradation case, rather than treating 150°C as a universal machine limit.

ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_hea.mechanism: At a given speed the illustrative compressor develops a flow-dependent head; changing speed shifts the head scale and flow domain.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_hea.implication: The operating point must satisfy both the compressor characteristic and the system pressure requirement, not a chosen point on the map alone.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_hea.recommendation: Intersect a validated map with the system curve and verify that all interpolation occurs inside the supported speed and flow range.

ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_eff.mechanism: Off-design flow increases internal aerodynamic losses relative to the best-efficiency region of the supplied map.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_eff.implication: The lowest-flow or highest-flow feasible point can consume more energy per unit product than operation near the efficient region.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_eff.recommendation: Compare speed control, recycle and parallel-train allocation using actual map efficiency and the required surge margin.

ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_ope.mechanism: Surge, high-flow choke, speed and driver limits bound different sides of a compressor’s usable operating region.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_ope.implication: An operating point inside one boundary can still violate another; a schematic envelope is not a manufacturer-approved safe operating area.
ch15_compressor_characteristics/ch13_ope.recommendation: Use validated boundary curves, include measurement uncertainty and test the anti-surge response independently of a steady-state map check.

ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_temperature_pr.mechanism: Counterflow transfers heat from the hot stream to the cold stream while maintaining a local temperature driving force along the exchanger.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_temperature_pr.implication: The plotted coordinate must use a consistent hot-to-cold spatial convention; an apparent temperature cross can be a plotting error or an infeasible specification.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_temperature_pr.recommendation: Check both terminal approaches and any internal pinch, and confirm hot-side enthalpy loss equals cold-side gain on the stated duty basis.

ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_duty_vs_flow.p.mechanism: Changing flow changes heat-capacity rate and residence time, so outlet temperatures and recovered duty respond together.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_duty_vs_flow.p.implication: The largest duty is not necessarily the best process result if the target outlet temperature or minimum approach is missed.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_duty_vs_flow.p.recommendation: Check temperature specifications and the energy balance for every flow case using newly evaluated inlet and outlet states.

ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_ua_sizing.png.mechanism: Increasing UA increases heat-transfer capability, but the streams’ heat-capacity rates and minimum approach ultimately limit recovered duty.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_ua_sizing.png.implication: Once the exchanger approaches its thermal limit, additional area offers progressively smaller energy benefit.
ch16_heat_exchangers/ch14_ua_sizing.png.recommendation: Select UA using the required outlet conditions, fouling allowance, pressure-drop limits and economics rather than extrapolating duty linearly with area.

ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_cv_and.mechanism: At fixed upstream and downstream states, increasing flow requires a larger valve capacity; the isenthalpic temperature change can remain almost independent of flow.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_cv_and.implication: Reusing an already sized valve can conceal the required-Cv trend, while constant JT cooling is physically plausible for identical inlet states and pressure drop.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_cv_and.recommendation: Size a fresh valve or clear its sizing state for each trial, then select hardware with rangeability and controllability across the full flow envelope.

ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_jt_coo.mechanism: A larger isenthalpic pressure reduction usually produces more cooling for the illustrated natural-gas state, with nonlinearity from changing fluid properties.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_jt_coo.implication: The coldest valve outlet can determine hydrate, low-temperature material and downstream separation requirements.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_jt_coo.recommendation: Calculate the full PH-flash path and check cold-start and low-flow inlet conditions rather than relying on a constant JT coefficient.

ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_pt_pat.mechanism: The pressure–temperature path follows constant stream enthalpy through an adiabatic valve rather than an isothermal or isentropic expansion.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_pt_pat.implication: Crossing saturation or hydrate boundaries can change the downstream phase load and operating risk even when pressure control is achieved.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_pt_pat.recommendation: Overlay the relevant phase and hydrate boundaries for the actual composition and evaluate the required temperature and pressure margins.

ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_valve_.mechanism: The trim characteristic maps valve travel to effective Cv; at imposed flow this changes the pressure drop required to pass the stream.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_valve_.implication: Valve opening is not a direct percentage of process flow, and very small openings can lie outside the feasible or controllable operating range.
ch17_valves_and_flow_control/ch15_valve_.recommendation: Check the chosen characteristic and fixed hardware Cv against both minimum controllable flow and maximum required capacity.

ch18_power_production/ch30_fuel_consumpt.mechanism: Fuel demand follows delivered shaft or electrical load, fuel heating value and the prime mover’s heat-rate or efficiency model.
ch18_power_production/ch30_fuel_consumpt.implication: Part-load efficiency and auxiliary loads can make fuel per unit product increase as production falls.
ch18_power_production/ch30_fuel_consumpt.recommendation: Use a validated heat-rate curve and consistent lower- or higher-heating-value basis, and separate generator output from useful process load.

ch18_power_production/ch30_power_demand_.mechanism: The power shares allocate the stated total among process consumers and auxiliaries; they represent the selected operating case.
ch18_power_production/ch30_power_demand_.implication: A demand breakdown identifies the largest consumers but does not prove that the generating system can serve them simultaneously.
ch18_power_production/ch30_power_demand_.recommendation: Reconcile every share with an equipment duty or stated assumption, then check generation, bus allocation and reserve requirements separately.

ch18_power_production/ch30_gt_ambient_te.mechanism: Warmer inlet air generally reduces gas-turbine air mass flow and available power while changing compressor and turbine performance.
ch18_power_production/ch30_gt_ambient_te.implication: The driver may reach its power limit on a hot day before the driven compressor reaches its own aerodynamic limit.
ch18_power_production/ch30_gt_ambient_te.recommendation: Use the package’s ambient correction data and assess the hottest design case, degraded condition and required spinning reserve.

ch18_power_production/ch30_co2_emissions.mechanism: Combustion CO2 follows fuel carbon consumption, while the operating-load dependence is shaped by prime-mover efficiency.
ch18_power_production/ch30_co2_emissions.implication: A shaft-load reduction does not necessarily yield the same percentage reduction in fuel or emissions, especially at part load.
ch18_power_production/ch30_co2_emissions.recommendation: Track absolute CO2 and emissions per unit product on a common fuel basis, and identify whether the inventory includes only combustion or also venting and fugitive methane.
